title: Live Social-Engineering Simulation - Virtual Environment
subtitle: Follow one attacker's full chain: Public Research (OSINT) → Spear Phishing Email → Fake Chat/SMS and Login Page → Fake Payment Request (BEC)
whyThisMatters: Real attacks rarely start with hacking. They start with a public profile on a professional networking site and a guessed email address. Watching the whole chain shows how normal each step looks on its own, and how dangerous they are together.
rememberThis: Keep this after today: one convincing message is never proof. Check using a channel the sender does not control.

discussionPrompts: Ask the group to spot, before you show the answer, which security layer would NOT have stopped this. One layer alone is not enough.
Ask how much of scenario 1's public data - name, job title, employer - they could find about themselves on a networking site right now.
For scenario 4, ask if anyone would feel able to say no to a "CFO" asking them to skip the normal payment checks.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: Many people think Email Security or the second login check on your phone (MFA — Multi-Factor Authentication) alone would have stopped the whole chain. The reveal shows no single layer covers all 4 stories. People most often miss the human layer — checking the address, the link, and the payment — which is the only layer that helps in 3 of the 4 cases.

intro.title: You are watching the attacker's screen
intro.body: This is a controlled, facilitator-led walkthrough. No real data was taken and no real email was sent. We will follow one attacker through 4 linked stories at a made-up company, Acme Corp. A public profile search (OSINT, open-source intelligence) and one guessed email become a spear phishing email (a fake message aimed at one person), a fake chat and SMS, and a fake CFO payment request (BEC, business email compromise). Use SPACE to go forward, LEFT ARROW to go back, and R to jump to lessons.

scenarios.title: Public Research (OSINT) & Email Guessing
scenarios.description: The attacker has no inside access, only public profiles. This is OSINT: collecting facts anyone can see. They list Acme Corp staff and guess the company email pattern.
scenarios.bridgeToNext: That guessed email is what makes the next step possible. Maya's inbox now gets a message built just for her.

sender.name: Acme Corp
sender.title: Public networking profile
sender.address: networking-site.example/company/acme-corp

beats.label: Networking Site Search

sender.name: Attacker Search Tab
sender.title: networking-site.example/search
sender.address: Search: "Acme Corp" - 1,247 employees

beats.text: Filter: Location=London, Title=Finance / Accounts Payable / HR. 18 profiles saved: 'Maya Patel · Accounts Payable Analyst', 'Daniel Reyes · CFO', 'Priya Nair · HR Coordinator' ... Job titles, join dates and cities are visible on public profiles.
beats.meta: Public data only - no login needed. Profiles show job title, employer and city. This step is called OSINT.

beats.label: Pattern Prediction

sender.name: Email Lookup Tool
sender.title: Public lookup — guesses from public pattern
sender.address: firstname.lastname@acmecorp.com — guessed pattern

beats.text: Pattern spotted from public Acme addresses: firstname.lastname@acmecorp.com. Guessed: maya.patel@acmecorp.com, daniel.reyes@acmecorp.com, priya.nair@acmecorp.com — 92% confidence. Accounts Payable inboxes are ideal: they handle invoices and bank details all day.
beats.meta: Attacker now has a valid-looking target list using only public information — no hack needed.

beats.label: Spear Phishing Email

sender.name: Staff Benefits
sender.title: benefits@acme-corp-benefits.com - EXTERNAL
sender.address: benefits@acme-corp-benefits.com via outside email service (not Acme)

beats.text: Subject: Updated Staff Benefits Summary | Hi Maya, please review your updated benefits summary and confirm your details via the staff portal link by 28 Nov. Warm regards, Staff Benefits - Acme Corp
beats.meta: Spear phishing: a fake message written for one named person. It looks like real Acme mail — only the address differs: benefits@acme-corp-benefits.com ("-benefits" added). Sent from an outside email service, not Acme — the sender check failed.

beats.label: Target Replies

sender.name: Maya Patel (External view)
sender.title: Re: Updated Staff Benefits Summary
sender.address: maya.patel@acmecorp.com → benefits@acme-corp-benefits.com

beats.text: Thanks! I've sent my employee ID and mobile number as requested. Let me know the next steps. - reply confirms the guessed address works.
beats.meta: One guessed email and one reply were enough. Attacker now has details that make the next 3 stories more believable.

holdPrompt.title: Pause - What was exposed before an email was even sent?
holdPrompt.body: Ask the group: what did the networking site already tell the attacker? Why is a named, public job title useful to them? Public profiles lead to guessed emails and messages that feel personal.

reveal.title: SCENARIO 01 - LESSON
reveal.subtitle: No hacking needed. Your public profile is the tool.

redFlags.label: Public Research (OSINT)
redFlags.detail: Employer, job title and city are public. A simple search can build a focused staff list in 10 minutes. No hack or breach needed — just public profiles.

redFlags.label: Predictable Email
redFlags.detail: firstname.lastname@acmecorp.com is easy to guess. One real pattern can predict hundreds of addresses.

redFlags.label: Lookalike Domain
redFlags.detail: benefits@acme-corp-benefits.com adds "-benefits". A real-sounding extra word makes it look genuine. Check the exact address, not just the display name.

redFlags.label: STOP, VERIFY, REPORT
redFlags.detail: Never send ID or personal details to an outside address. Confirm with the real team using the internal directory or the staff portal.

layers.name: Staff Awareness
layers.note: Staff trained to check the sender's exact address letter by letter would spot the added "-benefits" before replying with private details.

layers.name: Email Security
layers.note: A failed sender check plus a fake address sent from an outside service (not Acme) are exactly what email security is built to flag before it reaches your inbox.

reveal.callToAction: STOP: Is this information public? VERIFY: exact domain acmecorp.com. REPORT: it-security@acmecorp.com

scenarios.title: Fake Invoice & Document Lure
scenarios.description: Same trust, now the payload is a document Finance expects: an invoice or schedule. This is spear phishing with a malicious attachment.
scenarios.bridgeToNext: Email trust is used up. Next the attacker moves to channels with even less checking: workplace chat and SMS.

sender.name: Accounts Payable Inbox
sender.title: Accounts - Acme (Spoofed)
sender.address: accounts@acmecorp.com

beats.label: Legitimate Baseline

sender.name: Brightline Supplies
sender.title: accounts@brightlinesupplies.example - KNOWN VENDOR
sender.address: accounts@brightlinesupplies.example — sender check passed, known vendor

beats.text: Subject: Invoice 1042 — Feb 2025 & Delivery Schedule | Hi Maya, attached: Invoice_1042_Feb2025.pdf (480 KB) + Delivery_Schedule_Feb-Apr.xlsx (210 KB) — both from our billing system. No extra clicks needed. — Brightline Accounts
beats.meta: Expected files, matching icons, usual vendor tone. This is what you should see — a real invoice as a PDF and a schedule as a spreadsheet.

beats.label: Lure With Same Subject

sender.name: Brightline Supplies
sender.title: accounts@brightlinesupplies.example - SPOOF DISPLAY
sender.address: accounts@brightlinesupplies-secure.example (display masks as the real vendor)

beats.text: Subject: Updated Invoice — Please Review Immediately | Hi, Please find your updated invoice attached. Click 'Enable Content' to view the payment section. — Brightline Accounts
beats.meta: Subject reused, body vague, display name looks identical to the vendor — but the address behind it is different.

beats.label: Suspicious Payloads

sender.name: Attachments
sender.title: 2 files - password prompt
sender.address: Invoice_1042.pdf.exe (1.1 MB — actually an app, not a PDF) + Documents.zip (3.4 MB, password: 1234)

beats.text: Icon: blue app icon + purple ZIP icon. Banner: 'Enable Content / Enter password to view files'. File names are generic, sizes do not match a real invoice, and a password is given in the email body.
beats.meta: Double ending .pdf.exe — the last part (.exe) means it is actually an app, not a PDF. Generic ZIP plus "Enable Content" was not in the real invoice email.

beats.label: If Clicked

sender.name: Office Computer
sender.title: If you clicked Enable Content
sender.address: Finance laptop — hidden script tries to contact outside server

beats.text: If you click Enable Content, the document runs a hidden script that quietly tries to contact the attacker's server on the internet. From there, the attacker could reach staff details and bank information stored on the shared drive. All you would see is a message saying 'Document ready'.
beats.meta: Finance holds sensitive payment and bank data — one enabled file can put many colleagues at risk.

holdPrompt.title: Pause - Which file would you open?
holdPrompt.body: Show both inboxes side by side: expected PDF and spreadsheet versus .pdf.exe and ZIP. Ask who handles invoices daily and what "expected" means for them.

reveal.title: SCENARIO 02 - LESSON
reveal.subtitle: Vendors and colleagues are trusted senders. Attackers copy their stationery.

redFlags.label: Unexpected Type
redFlags.detail: An invoice never comes as .exe or ZIP with a password. PDF (480 KB) versus Application (1.1 MB) is visible in the file list.

redFlags.label: Double Extension
redFlags.detail: Invoice_1042.pdf.exe - the final .exe is the real type. Windows hides known endings by default.

redFlags.label: Enable Content Trap
redFlags.detail: "Enable Content" or "Enter password 1234" is what runs the attack. Real invoices say "No extra clicks needed" and never ask for a password.

redFlags.label: STOP, VERIFY, REPORT
redFlags.detail: Did you expect this file? Call the sender on a known number. Do not reply to an outside address with documents.

layers.name: Email Security
layers.note: Attachment scanning would flag a double ending like .pdf.exe or a password-locked ZIP that hides its contents before it reaches your inbox.

layers.name: Device Protection
layers.note: A file that tries to run a hidden script and contact an outside server is exactly what device protection (virus protection on the computer) is built to catch and block, even after the file is opened.

reveal.callToAction: STOP before you enable. VERIFY the file type and whether you expected it. REPORT to IT. Do not forward.

scenarios.title: Fake Chat, SMS & Login Page
scenarios.channelSummary: SMS • Workplace Chat (External) • Login Page Link
scenarios.description: People check phones and chat quickly and trust short messages. The attacker moves to SMS (smishing) plus a chat message from an "outside" account, pointing to a fake login page.
scenarios.bridgeToNext: Chat and SMS created fake urgency and made "do not check" feel normal. Now the attacker uses that: pretending to be a senior person to ask for money.

sender.name: IT Helpdesk (External)
sender.title: Workplace chat - External User
sender.address: Chat: Unknown user (external) - no history, generic avatar

beats.label: SMS Smish

sender.name: SMS - Acme IT
sender.title: From: ACMEIT (spoofed sender ID)
sender.address: +44 20-xxxx (via spoofed SMS gateway, no reply)

beats.text: Acme IT: Your staff portal is locked. Verify via: bit.ly/Acme-Portal-Verify or your account will be suspended. - IT Helpdesk
beats.meta: Smishing: a fake SMS. Shortened link, generic 'IT Helpdesk', sent at 06:12 when people check phones first thing.

beats.label: External Chat Message

sender.name: IT Helpdesk
sender.title: Chat - External (No org tag)
sender.address: it.helpdesk.3268@freemail.example invited you - 'External' banner, no chat history

beats.text: Hi Maya - quick one on your portal access. Can you confirm your login via the staff portal link below? When you have a moment. Thanks!
beats.meta: External chat: no @acmecorp.com tag, generic 'IH' avatar, external invite - easy to miss when you are busy.

beats.label: Link Mismatch

sender.name: Link Preview
sender.title: portal.acmecorp.com (display)
sender.address: Display: https://portal.acmecorp.com/staff/confirm

beats.text: Button shows: https://portal.acmecorp.com/staff/confirm - Actual href on hover/long-press: https://portal-acmecorp-secure.net/staff/verify?id=42 + alt bit.ly/Acme-Portal-Verify
beats.meta: Display: the real portal address. Actual link: a lookalike with an extra '-secure.net'. The page behind it is a fake login page built to steal your password.

beats.label: Pressure Nudge

sender.name: Follow-up SMS
sender.title: Anonymous
sender.address: Same +44 gateway - 'Don't call your manager, use link only'

beats.text: Reminder: Use the link only - your manager is out of the office and won't respond today. Portal closes 18:00.
beats.meta: Second channel reinforces the first (SMS + chat). 'Don't verify' is the attacker's defence against your best control.

holdPrompt.title: Pause - How many of you would tap on a busy morning?
holdPrompt.body: External chat plus SMS plus short link, all in a hurry. Ask the group: how do you check before you tap?

reveal.title: SCENARIO 03 - LESSON
reveal.subtitle: Busy and trusting is the target. Attackers add a second channel to drown out your check.

redFlags.label: Smished Link
redFlags.detail: bit.ly/Acme-Portal-Verify - IT never sends portal links by short SMS at 06:12. Short links hide the fake address.

redFlags.label: External Chat Account
redFlags.detail: "External" banner plus a free email address plus no history plus generic avatar = not IT Helpdesk. Real internal chat always shows @acmecorp.com and your org tag.

redFlags.label: Display ≠ Href
redFlags.detail: Display text can be faked. Press and hold or hover to see https://portal-acmecorp-secure.net. It has extra "-secure.net".

redFlags.label: STOP, VERIFY, REPORT
redFlags.detail: Use a bookmarked portal, or call the IT Helpdesk on a known number. Never use "link only".

layers.name: Staff Awareness
layers.note: Seeing the "External" chat banner with no org tag and hovering over the link to see the wrong destination is a human catch, not a technical one.

layers.name: MFA / Login Security
layers.note: Even if your portal password was entered on the fake page, the second check on your phone (MFA — Multi-Factor Authentication) would stop it from working on the real account.

reveal.callToAction: STOP before you tap. VERIFY the link destination and chat org tag. REPORT the external chat user and SMS sender.

scenarios.title: Boss Impersonation & Fake Vendor Payment (BEC)
scenarios.description: Last step: after collecting public data, attachments, and chat trust, the attacker uses a senior identity to ask to skip a check. This is BEC (business email compromise): fraud that uses a fake boss or vendor to move money.

sender.name: Daniel Reyes
sender.title: Chief Financial Officer — Acme (name display is fake)
sender.address: Display shows 'Daniel Reyes — CFO' but real address is d.reyes.acme@freemail.example (outside personal email, not @acmecorp.com)

beats.label: CFO Urgent DM

sender.name: Daniel Reyes
sender.title: Chief Financial Officer — Acme (display name is fake)
sender.address: Real address: d.reyes.acme@freemail.example (outside personal email) — display pretends to be 'Daniel Reyes — CFO'

beats.text: Hey - sorry for the early ping. Confidential supplier matter - need your help before my 09:00 board call. Keep strictly between us for now.
beats.meta: The display name and title look internal, but the address behind it is an outside personal email (not Acme). Sent before business hours to pressure you.

beats.label: Authority + Secrecy

sender.name: Daniel Reyes (CFO)
sender.title: CFO — Acme (fake display)
sender.address: Same outside personal email — 'This comes directly from me. Keep between us — I will explain once it is done.'

beats.text: This comes directly from me as CFO. Please keep it strictly between us for now - I'll explain everything once it's done. Don't loop in the Finance team until confirmed.
beats.meta: Authority + secrecy: two classic social-engineering levers, especially effective on junior staff.

beats.label: External Vendor Invoice

sender.name: Vendor - Brightline Supplies
sender.title: accounts@brightlinesupplies.example - EXTERNAL
sender.address: accounts@brightlinesupplies.example (external vendor) - CC: Daniel Reyes

beats.text: Subject: UPDATED Bank Details - Brightline Supplies - INV-84271 | Hi, our bank details have changed for this month's settlement (USD 48,500). Please remit to A/C 00123456 - Example Bank by 15:00 today, or supplies will be delayed. - Brightline Supplies
beats.meta: External entity pivots here: vendor email supplies the fraudulent bank details, the fake CFO provides the authority to use them.

beats.label: The Wire Ask

sender.name: Daniel Reyes (CFO)
sender.title: CFO - Urgent
sender.address: Same fake address — 'Wrap in next 10 min — board call then unreachable. Process payment $48,500 now — do not check with Finance until confirmed.'

beats.text: Please process a wire transfer of $48,500 to the account in the vendor mail right now - and don't loop in Finance until it's confirmed done. I'm about to go into a board call and won't be reachable after that.
beats.meta: Time pressure + financial request outside normal channels + "do not check" — completes the chain that started with a public profile search on Day 1.

holdPrompt.title: Pause - What actually stops a fake CFO order?
holdPrompt.body: A "CFO" display name plus outside vendor invoice plus 10-minute deadline. Ask Finance: what breaks this chain?

reveal.title: SCENARIO 04 - LESSON
reveal.subtitle: No real CFO skips Finance checks. The chain is the point.

redFlags.label: Fake Name Display
redFlags.detail: "Daniel Reyes — CFO" is just display text at the top. The real address behind it is d.reyes.acme@freemail.example — a free personal email, not @acmecorp.com. A real Acme leader never uses a personal email for a payment.

redFlags.label: Urgency + Unreachability
redFlags.detail: "Next 10 min, then board call - not reachable." Fake deadline to stop you from calling back to check.

redFlags.label: Outside Bank-Detail Change
redFlags.detail: A vendor bank-detail change was sent via an outside email copied to the fake leader. Real changes use the vendor portal plus a call back to the vendor on a number you already have. Never email plus chat alone.

redFlags.label: STOP, VERIFY, REPORT
redFlags.detail: STOP: private plus urgent. VERIFY: call the CFO and vendor on known numbers. REPORT: to Finance and IT. Do not pay.

layers.name: Staff Awareness
layers.note: Seeing that no real CFO asks you to skip Finance checks, and calling back on a number you already know instead of the one in the message, is a human catch.

layers.name: Incident Response
layers.note: Flagging the request to skip checks instead of acting on it is what stops the payment. This is Finance's own reporting step.

reveal.callToAction: STOP: outside plus private. VERIFY with known CFO and vendor numbers. REPORT - this is exactly why Finance has a separate approval chain.

globalReveal.title: FULL FLOW - How 4 scenarios become one fraud
globalReveal.subtitle: Public research (Day 1) to fake attachment (Day 4) to chat/SMS (Day 5) to fake payment (Day 6) — same attacker, same guessed email

redFlags.label: Chain, Not One-Off
redFlags.detail: Each step helps the next: public profiles lead to a guessed email, then a fake invoice, then chat trust, then fake CFO authority plus a vendor bank change.

redFlags.label: Your Breaks
redFlags.detail: Domain check (Day 1-2), attachment check (Day 4), link hover plus chat org tag (Day 5), call back plus approval chain (Day 6).

globalReveal.layersIntro: Different layers stopped the chain at different points. No single control would have stopped all of it.

layers.name: Staff Awareness
layers.summary: Caught the fake address (S1), the external chat tag and link mismatch (S3), and the authority and urgency request to skip checks (S4). The most consistent catch, but never enough alone.

layers.name: Email Security
layers.summary: Flagged the fake sending address and sender-check fail (S1) and would have blocked the fake attachment (S2). But SMS, Teams, and the final payment request never use email.

layers.name: MFA / Login Security
layers.summary: Would have stopped stolen portal passwords from working on the real site because the second check on your phone was still needed (S3). Only one step in the whole chain involved logging in.

layers.name: Device Protection
layers.summary: Would have blocked the hidden script that tried to contact an outside server after the attachment was opened (S2).

layers.name: Network Firewall
layers.summary: Not used. Nothing in this chain relied on a network break-in that a firewall would see.

layers.name: Backup & Recovery
layers.summary: Not used. This chain steals trust and money, not data, so there is nothing here that recovery would undo.

layers.name: Incident Response
layers.summary: Finance's own reporting step — flagging the request to skip checks instead of acting on it — is what stops the payment before it is sent (S4).

globalReveal.callToAction: For every role - Finance, HR, IT, managers - STOP (private and urgent), VERIFY (known address, number, or portal), REPORT (IT and manager).
